articles.title: DOUG SCHOEN: Why Democrats cannot break free from the far left’s transgender demands
articles.summary: From Seth Moulton's debate reversal to Byron Donalds' attacks in Florida, transgender policy is emerging as a central issue in 2026 midterm campaigns.
articles.body: The most formidable challenges facing establishment Democrats in November’s midterms are the success of far-left, socialist, or progressive candidates in primary elections and mainstream Democrats’ surrender to that wing of the party. Alongside advocating for an agenda that is radical in its drive to reshape America – and is broadly unpopular – the DSA’s influence has left Democrats on the wrong side of an issue that the party has been hobbled by in the past: transgender policies. Simply put, the DSA’s strong opposition to legislation banning biological males from competing in women’s sports has come to define where the national Democratic Party stands, much to its detriment. FORMER BERNIE SANDERS OPERATIVE WARNS RADICAL LEFT HAS 'OVERTAKEN' THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY FROM WITHIN And while this problem did not suddenly become an issue – Democrats had been trending this way for years before the 2024 election – it is only getting worse and will continue to do so. Indeed, we have already seen examples of it becoming a prominent topic in 2026 campaigns. DEMOCRATS STAY QUIET ON NEXT STEPS AFTER SUPREME COURT TRANSGENDER SPORTS RULING In Florida, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds has made transgender issues a central line of attack against Democrat David Jolly, including Jolly’s position on gender-affirming care for minors. Jolly disputes Donalds’ characterization of his position. Moreover, in Massachusetts, during a debate against incumbent Democratic Sen. Ed Markey, primary challenger Rep. Seth Moulton was forced to reverse himself and walk back comments he made just two years ago. MASSACHUSETTS SENATE CANDIDATES TRADE SHARP ATTACKS IN FIERY DEBATE AS INCUMBENT MARKEY SKIPS EVENT At the time, Moulton said, "I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete." Fast-forward to their 2026 debate earlier this month: Moulton walked back his phrasing, apologizing to the trans community for any pain caused while insisting his underlying goal was to encourage open debate within the party. BATTLEGROUND DEMOCRAT FLIP-FLOPS ON CONVERSION THERAPY AFTER LEFT-WING BACKLASH Does Moulton now fear more for his primary prospects with an increasingly dominant far-left base than he does for his daughters’ safety? Both of these examples show the pressure Democrats face from their left flank and their refusal to distance themselves from a position the American people and most Democrats do not endorse. HOUSE DEMS HAND GOP A WIN ON TRANS SPORTS AS PARTY UNITY CRACKS Analyses of the 2024 election compellingly suggest that this could well have played a decisive role in the outcome. The DNC’s post-election autopsy "determined [Kamala] Harris had no answer" to "Republicans’ very effective advertisements" highlighting Harris’ position. NEVER-TRUMP REPUBLICAN IS TOP DEM CHOICE IN CRUCIAL FLORIDA PRIMARY Further, according to one PAC’s analysis, then-candidate Donald Trump’s "Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you" ad was so effective that it shifted the race almost 3 points in Trump’s favor, double his 1.5 percentage-point margin of victory in the popular vote. The Trump campaign also pointed to the ad’s success with suburban women, a key demographic. DEMOCRATIC INFIGHTING GROWS AS CONGRESSWOMAN EXPOSES ‘DISRESPECTFUL’ WELCOME OF SOCIALISTS INTO ‘BIG TENT’ Make no mistake, Democrats are on the wrong side of the transgender debate given public opinion. According to Gallup’s May 2025 survey, roughly 7 in 10 (69%) Americans – including 72% of independents and a plurality of Democrats – believe transgender athletes should only be allowed to play on sports teams that match their gender at birth. Even among Democrats, support for allowing transgender athletes to play on teams that align with their current gender identity has dropped 10 points since 2021, now sitting below a majority, at 45% – despite party leadership’s embrace of the position. Pew found that 49% of Americans favored requiring transgender people to use public bathrooms matching their sex at birth, while 26% opposed such policies. Americans continue to support laws that would require transgender people to use public restrooms that match their sex at birth, not the one to which they have transitioned. However, when it came time to actually take a stand, no Democratic senators and just two Democratic House members supported a 2025 bill that sought to bar transgender athletes from competing against girls in K-12 schools. DEM REP HENRY CUELLAR REJECTS DSA AGENDA, SAYS SOCIALISTS ARE TRYING TO 'USE' DEMOCRATIC PARTY To that end, neither Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer nor House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been willing to take specific positions aligning with popular views favoring bans on transgender athletes competing in women’s sports. Schumer has been the most explicitly opposed to the bans, calling them "despicable," while Jeffries has been more measured, simply saying that Democrats care about "fairness in sports" but refusing to support legislation seeking to bar the practice. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION In Maine, Gov. Janet Mills has publicly clashed with the Trump administration over the state’s policy allowing transgender students to participate in school sports according to their gender identity. Ultimately, despite broad public opposition to allowing transgender athletes to compete according to their gender identity – and a sharply divided Democratic electorate – the party’s elites continue supporting policies allowing this to occur, or at best equivocate. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP At the same time, the data make clear the dilemma establishment Democrats face: continue mollifying the far left, or risk having the transgender issue hurt the party in general elections. Put another way, the far left’s and DSA’s veto over Democratic policy puts the entire party on the wrong side of another key issue. And unfortunately, all signs point to this problem continuing to be a drag on Democratic support in the midterms and into the 2028 presidential election. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DOUG SCHOEN

articles.title: Chinese government ships spotted in record numbers off Taiwan in July
articles.summary: China is ramping up pressure on Taiwan, with Beijing sending a record number of government vessels to waters around the island last month, according to figures provided by Taiwan’s coast guard.
articles.body: China is ramping up pressure on Taiwan, with Beijing sending a record number of government vessels to waters around the island last month, according to figures provided by Taiwan’s coast guard. The 244 sightings of Chinese government vessels – ships belonging to the China Coast Guard, scientific research agencies and others – was more than four times the number seen in July 2025, Taiwan’s coast guard said. That amounts to about eight ships a day, the official figures show. China “is escalating its campaign to bring Taiwan’s surrounding waters under its jurisdiction and may be testing the willingness of foreign vessels to comply with (Chinese) authorities in disputed waters,” the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) think tank said in an analysis earlier this month. The numbers do not include Chinese vessels in waters near Taiwan’s offshore islands, including Kinmen, Matsu and Pratas, the coast guard said. If those are added, the number almost doubles, to 425. That compares to 233 Chinese ships last July. The number of Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy warships in waters around Taiwan is also not included in the tally. A Taiwanese official said last month that the activity points to a critical wartime risk: that Beijing may be rehearsing how to sever Taiwan’s Pacific supply lines. “If the situation escalates to a blockade — which would amount to a quasi-war — we have plans to work with the navy to jointly protect Taiwan’s lifeline sea routes,” the official told CNN. Though Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy, Beijing has vowed to bring the island under its control – by force if necessary. Earlier this summer, the movement of ships from China’s Maritime Safety Agency (MSA) – a law enforcement rather than military organization – to Pacific waters east of Taiwan was noted by analysts and Chinese state media. China’s state-run tabloid Global Times called the movement of the MSA ships “a sovereignty declaration with both legal significance and political signaling.” Taiwan’s coast guard said at the time that the Chinese law enforcement ships were issuing radio challenges to the vessels heading to Taiwan. A Taiwanese official last month said that while the Chinese coast guard vessels have so far not boarded merchant ships passing through waters around Taiwan, they have broadcast questions to these vessels about port entry and exit information to create the false impression that Beijing has jurisdiction over waters around Taiwan. Such broadcasts have “already put pressure on these commercial ships,” although none of these vessels had changed course,” the official said. According to the Institute for the Study of War, China earlier this month used a typhoon in the region to try to test MSA control of ships in the area. “The MSA announcement said that passing ships must ‘strictly comply with traffic control requirements’ and ‘obey the instructions of on-site maritime management agencies,’” the ISW report said. And they are just the latest application of China’s gray-zone tactics, it says. China “likely intends to expand its de facto control around Taiwan as much as possible through means short of war, which erodes Taiwan’s sovereignty, strains Taiwan’s resources, and sets favorable conditions for future (Chinese) military operations against Taiwan,” it says. Taiwan legislature approves $7 billion for drones Taiwan’s opposition-controlled legislature approved a plan on Thursday to spend more than $7 billion on unmanned systems (including UAV, USV and UUV) over the next six year. The planned purchase indicates Taiwan’s learning lessons from the armed conflicts in Ukraine and Iran to hopefully deter an attack by China, while at the same time turbocharging its domestic drone industry. Taiwan has launched an islandwide effort to bolster its drone production with an aim to become world leader. In just the first seven months of this year, it exported roughly 2.6 times more drones in value than the entire 2025, according to Taiwan’s official trade data.

articles.title: 'Not far enough' - parents and teens on Meta's new limits for young users
articles.summary: As part of an $18bn settlement in a child-safety lawsuit, Meta announced new restrictions on its apps. We asked families what they thought.
articles.body:
For Elizabeth Cardner, a mother of two girls in Houston, Texas, Meta's new limits on how teenagers can use its platforms are a welcome sign that more people are aware of social media's potential dangers.

But, she tells the BBC, they probably won't help much in the long-term.

"It will save a few arguments at home, but it doesn't go far enough," she says.

This week, Meta announced new restrictions on its platforms - which include Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - as part of an $18bn (£13.25bn) settlement with US states in a lawsuit on social media's effects on children.

The company said it would set a daily two-hour time limit, hide the number of likes that a post receives, remove autoplay on videos, mute push notifications during school hours, and ban extreme make-up filters.

It also announced changes to its age-verification process and parental controls as well as agreeing to appoint an independent auditor to check the measures are implemented and maintained.

Many parents across the US see the restrictions as helpful, but are still sceptical. Those who spoke to the BBC described feeling stuck - where they feel they can't cut their children off from social media but also can't protect them from the harms they believe it causes - and they are waiting to see how much of a difference these new rules will make.

Cardner's 14-year-old, Paige, believes the restrictions will lead to "more real-life scenarios" and less "fake content", which she says dominates social media. She and her sister both approve of hiding the numbers of likes and restricting filters.

But Paige sees those gains as short-lived, "since AI is evolving".

"People will find new ways to have fake filters, and correct certain parts of their videos or pictures," she says. "So I think it'll help until people use other resources to try and find new ways to do that."

Cardner says banning her daughters entirely from social media would only result in them being left out by their peers.

"Damned if you do, damned if you don't," she says. "I don't think there's any winning on it."

What the Meta settlement means for the UK, and other questions after the deal

Meta's $18bn settlement may hasten reckoning for social media on child safety

Meta to pay up to $18bn to settle claims its platforms harm children

Another mother of two teens, Andria Rose, told the BBC that she feels defenceless and "no matter how much I protect my kids, Facebook, Instagram - they're coming in and literally, like, taking them out of their rooms".

Even though she calls Meta's changes "fantastic", Rose, who lives near Boston, Massachusetts, doesn't believe they are fully addressing the problem.

"They're trying to limit the drug, but they're not controlling the drug," she says. "They're still dealing."

Rose notes her personal use of social media costs her sleep at night.

"I'm hooked," she says. "So what do you think is going to happen to a kid?"

The settlement was announced on Wednesday in the middle of a highly-anticipated trial, where Meta owner Mark Zuckerberg was expected to testify. The settlement did not include any admission of fault.

The lawsuit was originally filed in 2023 by 29 US states, alleging Meta deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive and lied about risks. They also accused it of violating a federal law on collecting children's personal information.

The settlement - announced this week - included 48 states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories.

Several studies have found social media to be harmful to mental health, especially for children. Last year, a BBC investigation found children were being exposed to content about bullying, suicide and weapons on social media platforms.

For Rose, Meta's settlement payment "is like throwing a couple of dollar bills at a problem", given how much money the company makes and how much she believes the industry profited from children during the pandemic.

Joanie Story, a mother of four boys in Long Island, takes issue with another part of Meta's announcement - its conditions involving other platforms.

The company will withhold $5bn of the settlement, and only release it if YouTube, TikTok and others also enter into similar agreements.

It also said it would further tighten its time limit to one hour if other platforms implement similar restrictions. Story sees that as "petty".

"That's like saying: 'You know, we have the ability to fix what is broken, but we're only gonna fix it halfway,'" she says.

Still, Story is greeting the new rules as "good controls". She says she saw what a lack of controls could do when two of her sons were accidentally exposed to explicit content on a non-Meta platform. One boy has been in therapy for four years, she says.

"It's almost like being abused," says Story.

Mark SooHoo, a father of three who lives in the suburbs of Chicago, says social media and smartphones go hand-in-hand, and that both are harmful to young people.

He belongs to Wait Until 8th, an organisation where parents pledge to not give their kids smartphones until the end of eighth grade, when most have finished middle school and are 13 or 14 years old.

Most parents want to give their children smartphones so they aren't left out, he says.

"And our message is very clear: We do want them to be left out. We want them to be left out of all the negative impacts of social media," SooHoo says.

Instead of looking to the companies to address potential harms, SooHoo believes more parents should sign the smartphone pledge.

"A communal problem requires a communal solution," he says.

articles.title: Meet Reyha Raghavaraju, the 16-year-old Georgia student who turned her love of baking into birthday celebrations for more than 136 families in need across metro Atlanta
articles.summary: US News: A birthday cake can seem like a small thing, a kind gesture. But for a child whose family is struggling to make ends meet, having one can mean far mor.
articles.body: A birthday cake can seem like a small thing, a kind gesture. But for a child whose family is struggling to make ends meet, having one can mean far more than a slice of cake and a candle. Sixteen-year-old Reyha Raghavaraju saw that firsthand at a food distribution event in Georgia. She noticed a child wearing a birthday hat, but there was no birthday celebration waiting for them.The sight stayed with her. "This one kid was wearing a birthday hat," Raghavaraju said. "And then I asked him what he was doing for his birthday and he's like, 'I'm here,'" she told CBS News. The Alpharetta teenager who loved baking, began wondering if something as simple as a homemade cake could help children in families facing financial hardship feel celebrated on their special day.That question eventually became Birthday Bundles, a youth-led initiative through which Raghavaraju has helped bring birthday celebrations to more than 136 families across metro Atlanta.She started with what she already lovedReyha did not set out to build a large charitable organisation. She started with something she already knew and enjoyed doing, baking. Instead of simply donating food, she began creating birthday packages designed to make the occasion feel like a real celebration. The packages can include homemade cakes or cupcakes, gifts and handwritten birthday cards. Raghavaraju said each bundle is created with the recipient in mind, including age-appropriate gifts and a personalised message.For a child, the difference can be significant. A cake means candles to blow out. A gift means something to unwrap. A handwritten card means somebody has taken the time to think about them. Her goal was not to create elaborate birthday parties or expensive celebrations. It was to make sure that financial difficulties did not completely take away the experience of being celebrated."I think the hallmark of Birthday Bundles is what we do for every single bundle: we have a handwritten card," Raghavaraju said. "So our handwritten cards, we write them all by hand."From one celebration to 136 familiesBirthday Bundles gradually expanded. As more people learned about the teenager's work, volunteers joined her. The effort now involves around a dozen volunteers and has reached more than 136 families in the metro Atlanta area, according to CBS News Atlanta.Fourteen-year-old Saira Sharma, Raghavaraju's longtime friend and neighbour, is one of the young volunteers helping prepare the cakes and bundles. The organisation currently works with three shelter partners, including Covenant House Georgia. One recent delivery included a homemade cake and birthday bundle prepared for young people served by the organisation.Raghavaraju said the experience has changed the way she thinks about something many families may take for granted. "To me, what was shocking is that they didn't get something as simple as a birthday celebration," she said.Birthday Bundles is now looking for additional volunteer bakers, donations and shelter partners as it works to expand beyond its current North Fulton volunteer base.A homemade cake may last only a few days. A present may eventually be outgrown. A cupcake will be eaten. But the feeling of being remembered can last much longer. For a child who might otherwise have had an ordinary day, receiving a birthday package can send a simple message: your birthday matters, and so do you.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Americans remain sour on Iran war and judge questions Kennedy Center renovations: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: After six months of war, Americans remain sour on President Trump’s handling of the conflict.
articles.body: After six months of war, Americans remain sour on President Trump’s handling of the conflict. How climate change likely played a role in the deadly Nepal-Tibet flood. And a coroner questions whether measles played a role in an infant’s death. Here’s what to know today. Americans doubted the Iran war from the start — and Trump’s numbers haven’t gotten better At the six-month mark of the Iran war, Americans remain sour on President Donald Trump’s handling of the conflict, even as Republicans continue to voice support for military action and the president himself. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Thanks for reading today’s Morning Rundown. Today’s newsletter was curated for you by Elizabeth Robinson. If you’re a fan, please send a link to your family and friends. They can sign up here. Reputable, nonpartisan polls conducted over the last few weeks have found Trump’s approval rating on his handling of Iran ranges from 25% to 35%. A July Fox News poll found that 34% of registered voters approved of Trump’s handling of Iran, roughly in line with CNBC’s July poll, which found 35% approval. A Reuters poll conducted a few days ago put Trump’s approval rating on Iran at 29%. While Americans have broadly disapproved of Trump’s handling of the conflict from the start, the recent lows represent a decline from his earlier polling on the issue. Just as the war began, an NBC News poll of registered voters found that 41% approved of Trump’s handling of the conflict, while 54% disapproved. In the same survey, 52% of registered voters said the U.S. should not have taken military action against Iran. That opposition has persisted. In the most recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, just 35% approved of the military action, while 62% disapproved. A closer look at what Americans think of the war. More politics news: The war was a topic of discussion in CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s surprise trip to Moscow this week. According to a U.S. official and an adviser to the Kremlin, Ratcliffe asked Sergey Naryshkin, the chief of Russia’s foreign intelligence service, that Moscow not share intelligence with Iran. Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” as the trade war between the U.S. and Canada escalates. What caused the glacier collapse that triggered the Nepal floods More than 500 people have been killed and more than 1,000 people are missing in the catastrophic floods that smashed through Nepalese villages. Families are waiting in agony to hear from their missing loved ones, and rescuers face difficult conditions to reach remote villages and search through thick layers of mud. Maps and satellite imagery show how a glacier collapse sent ice, rock and floodwaters surging into communities. The disaster marks the latest in a series of catastrophic events in the Himalayas linked to rising temperatures and shifting ice and rock at high elevations. While experts said the precise sequence of events may not become clear for days or even weeks, a prevailing theory has emerged. “The probability is almost 100% that this is permafrost,” said Wilfried Haeberli, a professor emeritus at the University of Zurich, adding that as climate change continues, “this will be even more serious.” Alton Byers, a faculty research scientist at the University of Colorado Boulder, explained that permafrost acts as the adhesive that keeps frozen slopes intact. When it thaws, gravity takes over. A closer look at the dangers the Himalayas face. Follow our live blog for the latest updates. Judge questions DOJ lawyers about Kennedy Center plans A federal judge said he is considering temporarily blocking the Kennedy Center board’s plans to add Donald Trump’s name to the performance venue, during a hearing in which he peppered a DOJ attorney with questions about the effort. The hearing came after a Justice Department lawyer suggested in a court filing this week that the center could be demolished if Trump’s name is not allowed to be added to the site. The Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board voted this month to add the words “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” to the building and rename the property “President Donald J. Trump Plaza” by Sept. 8. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper asked a DOJ attorney, “What’s magic about that date?” He also questioned why adding the president’s name to the building would not violate federal law. How the Trump administration responded. Coroner says it’s unclear if measles played a role in baby’s death This week, the Pennsylvania Health Department announced two deaths associated with measles, including an infant. That same day, Lancaster County Coroner Dr. Stephen Diamantoni said that the infant died shortly after birth from an internal hemorrhage and a “traumatic rupture” of the spleen. While Diamantoni said he found evidence of the measles virus in the infant’s lung tissue, it remained unclear whether measles played a role in the child’s death. The state’s health secretary, however, expressed confidence in her department’s conclusion that the death was “measles-associated,” a term that means there was epidemiologic evidence of a measles infection. Here’s what else we know so far. The announcement of the two measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania has triggered a flurry of political sparring, misinformation and confusion. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Gov. Josh Shapiro have traded jabs, with Kennedy suggesting the deaths may have been “fabricated” and Shapiro criticizing vaccine misinformation from the federal government. As the debate continues and cases rise, local officials worry the competing claims could sow confusion among parents deciding whether to vaccinate their children. Read more about the confusion and debate. Staff Pick: Who’s tracking the risks from peptides? In many cases, no one What struck me most while watching an FDA advisory committee meeting last month on peptides was how much we still don’t know about these compounds, which are surging in popularity online. There’s remarkably little data on what many of them actually do in people — or the risks they might carry. That led to a simple question: If someone were harmed by one of these unapproved peptides, would anyone know? To find out, we reached out to health regulators in every state, revealing a patchwork of oversight. Of the 35 states that gave us detailed responses, only two — Massachusetts and California — described systems requiring pharmacies that prescribe peptides to report serious adverse events involving the drugs. In many states, regulators may not learn about a problem unless someone files a complaint. My reporting helps explain why someone might not do that. Two people I spoke with who said they experienced frightening symptoms after taking peptides were reluctant to report them because they had bought the drugs online. So while peptides are becoming increasingly popular, we don’t know how many people are being harmed — or whether the handful of cases we hear about are isolated incidents or signs of something bigger. — Berkeley Lovelace Jr., health and medical reporter Read All About It King Harald V of Norway, who went into exile in the U.S. as a child during the Nazi occupation of his homeland, has died. articles.title: Amy Dowden says she can achieve anything after Celebrity Hunted
articles.summary: The Strictly Come Dancing star appeared on the latest series of the Channel 4 challenge show.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This story contains details of the winner(s) of Celebrity Hunted

Strictly Come Dancing star Amy Dowden has said winning Celebrity Hunted has helped her believe she can "achieve anything" following her battle with cancer.

The 36-year-old professional dancer won the latest series of the Channel 4 challenge show alongside Strictly's Carlos Gu, claiming a joint victory with actor Brian Conley and his daughter, comedian Lucy Conley.

The programme sees celebrities go on the run while an elite team of hunters tries to track them down, in aid of Stand Up To Cancer.

The joint victory marked the first time in the show's history that two pairs have managed to stay on the run without being caught.

It also marked a reunion for Dowden and Brian Conley , who were paired together on the BBC One dance programme in 2017.

The nail-biting finale saw the two pairs jumping on an extraction plane from a beach in north Wales, narrowly escaping the hunters.

Dowden was just 32 when she was diagnosed with grade three breast cancer in May 2023 , after finding a lump in her breast the day before her honeymoon.

She said: "Cancer took a lot away from me in the last two years but I truly feel I've got my confidence back and this has given me the belief I can go on to achieve anything.

"We got on to that plane, I was just like, 'celebrate!' I grabbed the champagne!"

The Welsh dancer made a return to the ballroom floor in 2025 , and has been candid about her experiences of the disease, including having a mastectomy, chemotherapy and fertility treatment.

She was put into an early menopause as a result of the treatment, which she opened up about in her BBC documentary Strictly Amy: Cancer And Me .

Following their victory, Dowden, who also has Crohn's disease , and Gu admitted that none of their fellow Strictly stars thought they would succeed.

"All the hard work we put in those two weeks all of a sudden made it so worth it.

"I think wanting to do this to raise awareness for cancer, I think, inspired us.

"We knew we were doing this not just for us but for everyone going through it who might be watching at home."

Among the hunters' team are police and military personnel who have access to CCTV footage, helicopters, drones, dogs, media campaigns and the latest cyber forensic technology.

Brian Conley said winning the series was "amazing", but wished his eldest daughter Amy and wife Anne-Marie could have also been there to experience it with them.

He said: "We thought we're just gonna have fun and as long as we get a few days under our belt, that would be OK.

Lucy Conley said she felt "pure joy and shock" when the pair managed to get on the plane and claim their victory.

She said: "Just before we ran to the plane, we're in the sand dunes and dad's like, 'There's no way I'll win. They'll pick me off, I'm an old man, you've got to do this for us'.

"I was so nervous and then I got on that plane, turned around and he was there. That was crazy!

"I'll never experience any feeling like that. It was just pure joy and shock.

"Nobody who knew we were doing it believed we would win! No-one had any faith in us. Everyone thought we were going to be bad."

articles.title: After King Harald V’s death, what comes next for Norway’s scandal-prone royals?
articles.summary: The death of a monarch can boost national unity, and support for the crown. Norway’s new King Haakon VIII will be hoping that sentiment rings true following the death of his father, King Harald.
articles.body: The death of a monarch can boost national unity, and support for the crown. Norway’s new King Haakon VIII will be hoping that sentiment rings true following the death of his father, King Harald who died Friday after 35 years on the throne, marking the latest blow for a family reeling from scandal. The royal clan was thrust into the global spotlight earlier this year, when Queen Consort Mette-Marit, Haakon’s wife of 25 years, made headlines for her past association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, while her non-royal son from a previous relationship stood trial for rape. The succession of scandals sparked an open discussion in the country about her suitability to the role of Queen, with some experts even laying out possible options for her withdrawal from royal duties. But past criticism seems to have softened of late. Instead, the death of Harald V, who was Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, could potentially mobilize a fresh wave of support and empathy for the clan, experts now suggest. “Maybe people will remember the Epstein scandal, but I think maybe the worst will fade away,” Kjetil Alstadheim, the political editor at Norway’s influential newspaper Aftenposten, told CNN. The late King’s death could also contribute to “helping the new King and Queen into their roles and their positions because of how people will gather around the institution and the family,” Alstadheim said. Or as Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre put it on Friday after the news broke, “a whole nation is in mourning.” Harald’s death was officially announced at an extraordinary Council of State meeting at Norway’s Royal Palace on Friday, as the full title of the new King was formally presented. Haakon chose to keep the personal motto “All for Norway.” In his first comments following the death of his father, Haakon thanked the Norwegian people for their “support and compassion for the Royal Family during this time.” Haakon, 53, previously reflected on the power of succession to boost a sense of unity when speaking about the death of his grandfather. “It made an impression on me,” Haakon told NRK, Norway’s public broadcaster, in 2023. “It did something, with the understanding of how this was going to be for me, and it was also a clear expression that people were happy with my grandfather and the institution.” “There was a change in my life” at that moment, he said. Controversial union Haakon met Mette-Marit in the late 1990s, and the pair married in 2001 at Oslo Cathedral in front of 800 guests and a TV audience of millions. At the time, Mette-Marit’s openness about what she described as a “wild life” in her youth was well-received, particularly among younger Norwegians. “It mobilized the younger generations who felt this was a modern monarchy, and they could identify with that,” Alstadheim previously told CNN. “She managed to build trust and be respected.” But others felt she was an unconventional addition to one of Europe’s oldest royal houses as a single mother and given her reputation for partying. Speaking about the early days of their relationship, Haakon described Mette-Marit as “confident and worldly.” “You notice when Mette enters a room,” Haakon told NRK. “The fact that she had a young child really only told me that she wasn’t afraid to take on commitment and responsibility.” A troubled stepson That young child would years later spark a major PR crisis for the royal family. In June, Marius Borg Høiby, 29, was sentenced to four years in prison after being found guilty of rape and domestic violence after a seven-week trial that further tarnished the family’s reputation. Høiby pleaded not guilty to the most severe accusations against him, including those of rape, while admitting to some lesser charges. He is currently under house arrest at Norway’s Skaugum royal estate as he awaits a court decision about whether an appeal will be considered, his lawyer Petar Sekulic told CNN. Around the same time as Høiby’s trial began, a second scandal erupted, this time implicating Mette-Marit herself. The Epstein files revealed that she had maintained extensive correspondence with the disgraced financier years after he had pleaded guilty to soliciting sex from a minor. She later expressed regret over the association, saying it did not “represent the person I want to be.” Royal historian Ed Owens said that as a result, the royal house had no doubt been brought into a “degree of disrepute,” with the family facing a “difficult moment ahead of them in terms of the succession.” One concern was the family’s “reduced capacity” due to a “lack of manpower,” Alstadheim said, referring to its severe shortage of working royals. It was announced earlier this year that Mette-Marit would temporarily step back from royal duties to undergo a lung transplant after she was diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, a chronic progressive lung disease with a poor prognosis, in 2018. But her absence has “put things into perspective for many people,” said Tove Taalesen, a royal correspondent for news outlet Nettavisen. “It doesn’t erase what happened, and it shouldn’t. But I believe there is more sympathy for her now,” she told CNN. “I am more interested now in who Mette-Marit will be, after everything she has been through, than in continuing to punish her for mistakes she has already acknowledged.” Despite the challenges ahead, the royal commentators agree this moment could be unifying for the country, and its support for the monarchy, with Owens calling it a “re-energising of national identity.” ‘A solid foundation’ Haakon, a more energetic King than most European royal houses can lay claim to with a passion for the outdoors, takes the helm of a monarchy that still enjoys substantial support among the public, even if the latest scandals have taken their toll. A poll in February, during Høiby’s trial, showed its popularity dropped to a record low, but has since recovered. Debates over abolishing or scaling back the institution, which occasionally flare up in the United Kingdom and other nations, are rare in Norway. It is Haakon’s natural ability to, as Alstadheim puts it, be “close to the people” that brings hope for the monarchy’s future, and its ability to modernize with the times. In 2023, Haakon said he often gets asked what he would have done if he wasn’t a royal. “I say I would have been a pro surfer on the World Tour,” he told NRK. The new King also holds a bachelor’s degree in political science from the University of California at Berkeley, and credits his experience there with introducing him to people from different backgrounds. “The Norwegian royal family has managed to modernize gradually,” Alstadheim said. “Building on the popularity of King Harald, Haakon will have a solid foundation for his reign.” Taalesen agreed. “I believe in him. And I believe the Norwegian monarchy will survive King Harald. That is, after all, the whole idea of a monarchy: the person changes, but the institution continues,” she added. The new King and Queen Consort have two children together, and the elder – Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, 22 – now becomes heir to Norway’s throne.

articles.title: Fears Dunwich Heath wildfire could reignite as hot spots remain
articles.summary: The National Trust says it has been working to locate areas of underground burning at Dunwich Heath.
articles.body:
Fears have been raised that fires could reignite at a nature reserve that was devastated during a huge blaze.

Large parts of Dunwich Heath and of neighbouring RSPB Minsmere on the Suffolk coast were destroyed by a wildfire that ripped through an area the size of 210 football pitches on 29 July.

The National Trust, which owns and manages Dunwich Heath, said its teams had found hotspots and patches of ground smoking, prompting fears that unidentified areas could reignite.

But Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service said there were no further operational requirements needed from its crews.

The National Trust said it begun its first phase of safety assessments earlier in the week.

It said the hotspots and patches of smoking ground indicated underground burning, and teams had been making use of thermal imaging devices to find these areas.

One of the National Trust's priorities is to check where the firebreaks - large strips of land cleared of trees and vegetation - were cut during the emergency response to help stop the spread of fire.

"The earth-moving machinery did a vital job as part of the fire control measures, but the speed and scale needed at the time has meant vegetation such as gorse, heather and parts of trees have been churned into the banked soil and sand," a spokesperson said.

"In places, this has created a charcoal kiln effect, which has retained heat.

"We're worried that if these areas aren't identified and become exposed to an oxygen source they may reignite - the fire service reported seeing exactly these 'flare ups' happen during the wildfire, so we know it's a very real concern."

At this time of year, following prolonged hot weather, it is usual for ground temperatures to average between 25-35C.

The National Trust said thermal imaging showed some places in the heathland were in excess of 65C.

It took almost two weeks before the fire service stood down from the scene.

At its peak, 120 firefighters were there, with all 35 of Suffolk's stations involved and many crews called in from other counties.

Nearby holiday parks had to be evacuated and local farmers volunteered to help create firebreaks and provide water.

The fire service is investigating the cause of the blaze, while there has been sightings of wildlife returning to the area.

A spokesperson for the service said Suffolk, including the Dunwich Heath area, remained at high risk on the wildfire severity index and it encouraged people to remain vigilant.

articles.title: Iran war mediators focus on reopening Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Mediators in the Iran war are stepping up efforts to get the Strait of Hormuz reopened, with Tehran agreeing to draw up a list of conditions to restore normal traffic after ⁠a Qatari emissary pressed the Iranians to respect freedom of navigation.
articles.body: DUBAI — Mediators in the Iran war are stepping up efforts to get the Strait of Hormuz reopened, with Tehran agreeing to draw up a list of conditions to restore normal traffic after ⁠a Qatari emissary pressed the Iranians to respect freedom of navigation. With the U.S. having disengaged from talks in favour of an economic pressure campaign, the prime minister of Qatar, a U.S. ally, met senior Iranian leaders in Tehran on Thursday, stressing the importance of returning to the pre-war status of open shipping through an international waterway. Qatar and Pakistan helped broker a memorandum of understanding in June that led to a ceasefire but that quickly unravelled due to disagreements between Iran and the U.S. over the strait, which handled 20% of pre-war global oil supplies. In his mission to Tehran ⁠on Thursday, Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said on X ​that ⁠he underscored to senior Iranian officials “the importance of respecting freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with international law”. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Friday described the talks with Al Thani as “creative”, and he renewed his appeal to the U.S. to stop putting military and economic pressure ⁠on his country and to resume negotiations. “Putting diplomacy back on track isn’t impossible. It hinges on U.S. understanding of one simple fact: pressure doesn’t work,” Araghchi said on ​X. Iran’s foreign ⁠ministry later issued a statement condemning the United States’ new economic ‌sanctions on the country, announced on Monday, as “state terrorism”. It also urged other countries not to join the sanctions, saying this would amount to “complicity in imposing one state’s unlawful will” on others. Iran prepares list of conditions After the U.S. and Israel launched the war six months ago, Iran threatened to strike any vessel ‌transiting the strait without its authorisation, driving down traffic and sending up the price of oil, providing Tehran ‌with leverage in the bargain. The U.S. wants the strait to remain an open international waterway. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Thursday Iran was preparing a list of conditions for reopening the strait. Speaking through an interpreter in an Al Manar TV interview, Rezaei said Iran had agreed with Oman on a shipping corridor through the strait, with parts of the route in Omani waters and parts in Iranian waters. ⁠Ships would use a designated central channel if the U.S. met Iran’s conditions, he said. In the past Iran’s conditions have included an end to the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports, compensation and removal of sanctions. It remained unclear whether Iran intended to amend those demands in a way that might be acceptable to Washington. Tehran and Washington have exchanged little more than bellicose statements in recent weeks, leaving the diplomacy to third parties. Trump declared the June MOU “over” on July 8 and has cranked up efforts to wreck Iran’s economy. Clearing sea mines U.S. military commanders say American forces have cleared sea mines from the strait that had been laid months ago by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. “Bottom line: today, international shipping lanes are open and momentum is building,” Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of the U.S. military’s Central Command, said in a video message posted on social media. U.S. ‌forces have in recent months helped 1,500 commercial vessels carrying nearly 750 million barrels of crude oil to transit the strait, Cooper said. Trump has repeatedly ​said the strait was open, but many vessels have opted against sailing through it because of Iranian threats, and ship tracking services have estimated activity ‌at roughly 5% to 15% of normal volumes. Preliminary shipping data released on ⁠Friday showed that only seven commodity vessels had transited the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, down from 17 a day earlier and below the 10-day average ⁠of 15. However, Gulf energy exporters have also been seeking to reduce their overreliance on the strait by investing billions of dollars in new infrastructure, from energy pipelines to ports. Trade is being redirected to Saudi ports on ‌the Red Sea and the United Arab Emirates’ eastern ​coast ports, though capacity is smaller. Oil prices held steady on Friday but were on ‌track for a weekly drop, amid what analysts said were signs that more ​oil was flowing through the strait despite the diplomatic stalemate and that producers were increasingly adapting to the new realities in the Gulf region.

articles.title: Trump picked a trade fight with Canada. US defense firms may pay the price
articles.summary: None of what Washington wanted on defense was ever going to be delivered by threat.
articles.body:
Washington went into last week’s trade talks with Canada looking for more than relief on dairy and alcohol. The administration wanted Ottawa to complete its F-35 purchase, buy American radar planes as part of joining President Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense project and grant the U.S. a right of first refusal on Canadian critical minerals.

By Saturday morning, the talks had collapsed . Fifty percent tariffs hit roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods, and Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada will retaliate “ dollar for dollar ” starting Sept. 8. The bigger loss for Washington, though, may show up well after those tariffs stop making headlines.

None of what Washington wanted on defense was ever going to be delivered by threat. A tariff can be imposed and enforced at the border. Completing the F-35 order, joining Golden Dome, opening Canadian mineral reserves to American companies are different. No Canadian government can be forced into them, because each one requires Ottawa to keep saying yes, year after year, as contracts get signed and budgets get voted. Squeezing Canada on trade doesn’t make that yes more likely. It makes those choices harder to defend in Ottawa.

The administration has spent years telling allies to spend more on defense. Canada is finally doing it: Carney says his government will put half a trillion dollars into defense investment over the next decade. Until now, roughly 70 percent of Canada’s defense spending has gone to U.S. suppliers. Carney’s new defense industrial strategy wants Canadian firms to capture that same share instead. The trade fight didn’t start that pivot, but it has strengthened the case for it.

The F-35 is the clearest case. Canada contracted for 88 aircraft, but Carney ordered the purchase reviewed after Trump’s first tariff offensive last year. Washington wanted reassurance in these talks that Canada would finish the buy. It left without it.

The minerals dispute cuts the same way. The Pentagon has good reason to want secure North American supplies instead of Chinese ones. But demanding privileged access while punishing Canadian industries with tariffs was never going to produce a deal. Carney has already rejected exclusive access and called deeper minerals cooperation one of the casualties of the failed talks.

Since 1956, the U.S.-Canada Defense Production Sharing Agreement has tied the two countries’ defense industries together closely enough that more than 110 Canadian companies have taken part in the F-35 supply chain. Washington built that arrangement, and benefited from it, because Canadian procurement usually reinforced an American-centered continental defense economy. That was the quiet assumption behind seven decades of cooperation: it didn’t need to be re-earned in every budget cycle.

The defense relationship was already showing strain before the latest talks collapsed. In May, the Pentagon suspended the Permanent Joint Board on Defense , which had coordinated U.S.-Canada military consultation since 1940 , citing Canada’s slow progress on defense spending and its stalled F-35 decision. That happened three months before last week’s collapse.

Golden Dome exposes the same problem from the other direction. Canada is already investing in NORAD modernization with new radar and surveillance for the northern approaches that any continental missile defense system would need. Canadian participation still requires Canadian consent and Canadian money. Tariff pressure doesn’t make that participation more likely. It makes routine cooperation look like something Ottawa has to keep defending politically.

No serious Canadian government is going to withdraw from NORAD. Geography leaves both countries with too much at stake. The real damage will show up in the next round of choices: aircraft, sensors, industrial partnerships, as Canada decides where a much larger defense budget actually goes.

Trump wanted Canada to shoulder more of its own defense burden. He may get exactly that. What his administration hasn’t reckoned with is how much of that new Canadian money will still flow south, after a year of tactics that turned dependence on the United States into a political liability in Ottawa.

Andrew Latham is a professor of international relations at Macalester College in Saint Paul, Minn., a senior fellow at the Institute for Peace and Diplomacy.

articles.title: Carney: ‘Naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario’
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday rejected President Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” explaining the history of the Great Lake’s indigenous name in a post on social media. “The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” Carney wrote…
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday rejected President Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” explaining the history of the Great Lake’s indigenous name in a post on social media.

“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” Carney wrote on the social platform X .

He noted that the name had been used for more than 400 years, predating the Canadian Confederation and the signing of the U.S. Declaration of Independence.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” the prime minister continued. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

Other Canadian officials also refused to adopt the Trump administration’s new name. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the body of water, which is shared by New York and the Canadian province of Ontario, will always be Lake Ontario in Canada.

“It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever,” he wrote on social media .

Trump signed an executive order Thursday to formally change the lake’s name to Lake America after first floating the idea earlier this week amid a trade war between the U.S. and Canada. His order changes the name for federal purposes but has no authority beyond the U.S.

The move follows a similar move on the first day of his second term, when he signed an order renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.”

Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports and separately threatened additional 50 percent tariffs on automotive imports and steel beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs effective Sept. 8, with Carney promising to match Trump’s latest tariffs “dollar for dollar.” Seafood, however, was later exempted from the looming taxes.

articles.title: Hundreds of migrants cross Channel in one day after 10-day lull
articles.summary: Nearly 500 people crossed the Channel in seven boats on Thursday - the first since 17 August.
articles.body:
Nearly 500 migrants have arrived in the UK in one day, in the first boats to successfully cross the Channel in 10 days.

The seven vessels that made the crossing were the first since 17 August when 250 people arrived.

Dinghies arrived in British waters until late into the night on Thursday, with 494 people being brought into the Border Security Command compound in Dover, Kent.

The total number is down overall this year, according to BBC Verify analysis of government data.

Some 16,391 migrants have crossed the Channel so far, down 43% on the same time last year, and a 17% drop from the same point in 2024.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has said she will not be "complacent" about the falling numbers, and that there is "more we must do".

"That is why I have boosted enforcement on the French beaches and overseas and introduced new legislation to tackle the pull factors that draw people here through unsafe and illegal routes," she added.

articles.title: Ugandan King Oyo Nyimba, once world’s youngest monarch, dies at 34
articles.summary: Oyo Nyimba, a Ugandan king, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the crown in 1995, has died aged 34, the prime minister of his kingdom announced.
articles.body: Oyo Nyimba, a Ugandan king, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the crown in 1995, has died aged 34, the prime minister of his kingdom announced. Uganda is a republic, ruled by an elected head of ‌state, but it has several traditional monarchies that still preside over their kingdoms as they were constituted in the pre-colonial period. Their political power is largely symbolic, but they wield enormous cultural and social influence. Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV was the King of Tooro, a small kingdom in Uganda’s west near the border with the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo. “It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that I announce the passing of His Majesty the Omukama of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV,” the prime minister of the kingdom, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, said in a post on X late on Thursday. The king died at around 10:00 p.m. local time on Thursday, Akiiki said, without revealing the cause of his death. Rukidi IV was crowned at just three years old on September 12, 1995 after the death of his father, Rukirabasaija Patrick David Matthew Kaboyo Olimi III. Balaam Barugahara, a minister in the ‌government ⁠of President Yoweri Museveni, said shortly before the announcement of the king’s death that he was receiving treatment in the US. “This is an immeasurable loss,” the prime minister said, adding the king, who was unmarried, had left an heir and that “continuity of the Crown is assured.” His death triggered an outpouring of grief across ⁠social media platforms in Uganda and widespread media coverage nationally. “Most devastating news! May His Majesty the King’s soul rest in eternal peace,” Bobi Wine, Ugandan pop star-turned-politician who is the country’s leading opposition leader, said ⁠in a post on X. In April, in a message to celebrate the King’s birthday, Tooro’s prime minister had said: “Our King is not distant from the realities of his people; he ⁠is part of this generation, part of this ecosystem, growing, learning, and leading… His youth is not a limitation; it is a strength. It brings energy, fresh perspective, and the courage to imagine a different future for Tooro.”

articles.title: Trump is writing a most favored nation clause that nobody signed
articles.summary: President Trump seems to think the United States should get the benefits of other countries’ bargains.
articles.body:
Trade agreements are bargains. President Trump seems to think the United States should get the benefits of other countries’ bargains. But if countries expect Washington to claim the best concessions later without paying for them, they have every reason to offer less in the first place, including to American negotiators.

That idea connects two unrelated fights with Brazil and Canada. In both, Washington objects that other countries give some trading partners better treatment than they give the United States. It increasingly calls that difference “ discrimination ”.

Start with Brazil. Brazil, independently and through Mercosur , has “ partial scope ” trade agreements with Mexico and India . Those lower tariffs on select products, meaning Mexican and Indian exporters sometimes pay lower Brazilian tariffs than their American competitors.

The U.S. Trade Representative made these “unfair, preferential tariffs” part of its Section 301 investigation of Brazil, complaining that Mexico receives preferences on more than 1,000 tariff lines and India hundreds more.

Partial-scope agreements sit awkwardly in the trading system, and Congress has long questioned whether they satisfy the World Trade Organization requirement that free trade areas cover “substantially all trade.” But Washington’s argument goes further, claiming that American exporters are disadvantaged because somebody else negotiated better treatment.

Now consider Canada. Canada has its own trade agreements. Under the Canada-European Union Comprehensive and Economic Trade Agreement , Europe negotiated preferential access for cheese. The United States negotiated a different dairy package under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

Yet, in invoking Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 against Canada, Washington has cited more favorable treatment for European cheese as evidence of discrimination against American commerce.

As Mona Paulsen has shown , even Section 338’s architects understood the limit that the United States cannot indefinitely claim whatever preference another country negotiated. And the recently collapsed U.S.-Canada negotiations reportedly foundered in part over an extraordinary U.S. demand concerning Canada’s future trade agreements.

Put Brazil and Canada together and a doctrine becomes visible: Washington is now using Sections 301 and 338 as a most favored nation clause its trading partners never signed.

Investment lawyers will recognize the concept. Bilateral investment treaties commonly contain most favored nation provisions . They promise American investors treatment no less favorable than third-country investors receive, and an American investor may claim better treatment subsequently granted to European or Japanese investors.

That might look like free riding. The country agreed to it. The most favored nation obligation was part of the original bargain. It could demand compensation, negotiate exceptions or refuse it.

That is not what is happening here. Brazil gives Mexico a tariff preference. Washington calls the resulting disadvantage unreasonable under Section 301. Canada gives European cheese preferential access, and Washington calls the difference discrimination under Section 338. Tariff threats then supply the enforcement.

This is retroactive most favored nation without consent. It is also free riding on concessions others paid for. Europe did not receive Canadian cheese access for nothing; it negotiated the Comprehensive Economic Trade Agreement and gave Canada concessions in return. Mexico’s preferences in Brazil reflect a reciprocal commercial bargain.

If Washington demands comparable treatment simply because American exporters face a competitive disadvantage, it gets the benefit without paying the negotiated price.

The postwar system has always held a tension between nondiscrimination and preferential trade, and the solution is settled. Most favored nation is the default, but qualifying free trade agreements can offer deeper preferences because their members undertake deeper reciprocal commitments.

The United States has benefited enormously from this exception. Mexican goods receive USMCA preferences that Brazilian goods do not. Washington does not automatically extend those benefits to countries complaining of less favorable treatment. Why should its trading partners?

If Washington wants the best treatment Canada later gives another country, there is a straightforward solution: negotiate for it. What Washington should not do is obtain through unilateral tariff statutes what it failed to obtain at the negotiating table.

That is a credibility problem as well as a free-rider problem. Why negotiate tariff schedules, exceptions and rules if Sections 301 and 338 can rewrite those bargains afterward?

The problem is especially acute if Washington now wants influence over Canada’s future trade agreements. That is less of a new idea than a widened one. USMCA already requires Canada to give notice before negotiating with a non-market economy , and lets any party terminate on six months’ notice. The August demand reached far beyond it, going from claiming the benefits of other countries’ bargains to controlling which bargains they strike.

Nor is this hypothetical. Washington’s Malaysia agreement requires consultation on any future agreement that could jeopardize American interests, a term never defined.

For decades, the United States told countries that preferential access had to be earned at the negotiating table. Trump’s doctrine is different: Give somebody else a better deal, and America may demand it too, or impose tariffs until you do.

That isn’t the conventional most favored nation, and it isn’t reciprocity. It is a most favored nation clause nobody signed, enforced by tariff threats.

Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University. Barry Appleton is interim director of the Balsillie Legal Advisory Centre at the Balsillie School of International Affairs and Co-Director of the Center for International Law at New York Law School.

articles.title: China property crisis: Why Beijing is moving away from the pre-sale model
articles.summary: News News: China on Friday unveiled a series of measures aimed at reducing property developers' reliance on funds collected from homebuyers before projects are c.
articles.body: China on Friday unveiled a series of measures aimed at reducing property developers' reliance on funds collected from homebuyers before projects are completed, as Beijing seeks to curb risks and restore confidence in its crisis-hit real estate sector.Under new guidelines issued by China's central bank and financial regulator, a homebuyer’s mortgage will be issued only after a housing project has been completed.Another set of guidelines requires local governments to promote the sale of completed homes to “fundamentally prevent delivery risks”, according to Reuters.Mortgage only after project completionChina's property developers have for decades relied on a pre-sale model, selling homes before they were ready for delivery to fund debt-fuelled and high-turnover operations.However, the model came under scrutiny after construction at some presold projects stalled following the property market meltdown in 2021, which drained developers' cash and triggered protests by homebuyers.The new policies could help address buyers' concerns about stalled projects, according to Zhang Dawei, an analyst at Centaline Property.The measures suggest that policymakers “understand the urgency to stabilise the property sector”, Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist of Pinpoint Asset Management, told Reuters.State news agency Xinhua, citing unnamed officials, said the old housing sales system, which relies mainly on pre-sales and rapid turnover, was no longer suitable.Banks to take greater role in project financingThe new measures also seek to make financial institutions more responsible for project financing.Guidelines issued by the People's Bank of China and the National Financial Regulatory Administration require each housing project’s financing to be linked to a lead bank. The bank will monitor project funds and either provide or organise loans.The measures also extend the maximum term for personal mortgage loans to 40 years from 30 years.Separate draft measures issued by the financial regulator reiterated the central government's call for financial institutions to meet property developers' “reasonable financing needs” and urged trust firms to treat private and state-owned developers equally while providing financing.China's securities regulator also pledged support for developers' financing, including through refinancing, mergers and reorganisation.Property crisis continues to weigh on economyChina's property sector entered a prolonged downturn after a government campaign to curb developers' heavy borrowing triggered a liquidity crunch.More than five years into the slump, home prices are still falling, while property investment continues to decline.Some stalled projects also remain unfinished after developers, including former industry leader China Evergrande, defaulted on their borrowings amid tighter financing rules and falling home prices.Jeff Zhang, an equity analyst at Morningstar, said the policies would likely favour larger developers with healthy liquidity, as they would face less pressure to quickly recover cash from projects.Centaline Property's Zhang Dawei said smaller developers with limited cash reserves could be more likely to exit the market or change their business models as the pre-sale model is phased out.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: The US is canceling its Arctic Report Card when it matters most
articles.summary: Any business, town or development group needs this data informing their decisions.
articles.body:
“With new opportunities opening up, and new challenges emerging, close cooperation on Arctic security and economic development among our nations is more important than ever”.

This May joint statement by the U.S. and allies underscores the rapidly growing importance of the Arctic to the U.S. and on the global stage. Yet, earlier this month, I, my fellow editors and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration personnel were informed that support for the Arctic Report Card — our flagship annual report since 2006 — is canceled.

The U.S. is an Arctic nation not simply by interest, but on the ground. Alaska, our Arctic state, contains roughly 18 percent of U.S. land area. The Alaska coastline itself is almost 20 percent longer than the contiguous U.S. coastline.

The Arctic is also the fastest warming region on the planet, and conditions on land and sea are rapidly changing . The effects are being felt across industry and fisheries, business and economic development, remote communities, security and military planning, as well as in hazard preparedness and response.

The fast and timely release of the Arctic Report Card, in December of the reporting year, is a critical strength, with the report card commonly acting as the first information source on the latest observations and facilitating rapid decision making.

Sea ice in September now only covers roughly half of the area that it did in the 1980s. This has quickly opened up key shipping routes, particularly the Northern Sea Route along the Russian Arctic coast. The use and development of the route is progressing quickly.

This year, at least six Chinese operators are planning for container and bulk shipping services to Russia and expanding further into Western Europe. South Korea is finalizing their first Arctic cargo ship, planning to trial the route this summer with a crossing speed half as long as the existing Suez Canal route.

With changing sea ice, security monitoring processes are also challenged to keep up, pushing NATO, for example , to rapidly progress to maintain monitoring of Russian military submarines. Increased Arctic activity by potential adversaries is prompting U.S. military ships to shadow Chinese research vessels.

Earlier this month, the European Policy Center recommended that the European Union revise their Arctic vision of a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous region to, instead, put security as the top priority. The Arctic Report Card acts as a bridge between raw data and usable insights, and its findings inform U.S. and international policy.

It has been cited by the U.S. Congressional Research Service , in NATO’s January report, “The Effects of Climate Change on Security,” the Arctic Council’s Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Program and others.

The push for economic and infrastructure development in the Arctic also requires accessible data and sound environmental intelligence.

The 2025 Arctic Report Card highlighted concerning new data on the increasing occurrence of “ rusting rivers ,” with more than 200 Alaskan watersheds showing signs of increased acidity and toxic trace metal contamination, impacting drinking water and fishing. Compounding environmental hazards are increasing risks for remote communities and industry development.

The report also discussed flooding and landslide hazards from the combined loss of glacier ice and permafrost thaw that is already damaging infrastructure. Without the protection of coastal sea ice, ocean waves easily remove land, and landslide risks are also increasing threats to life and property.

Any business, town or development group needs this data informing their decisions. By translating data points into usable environmental information via the efforts of approximately 100 contributing scientists from a dozen countries, those who most benefit from the Arctic Report Card are the non-scientists working on Arctic land and sea.

Our Arctic Report Card editor team and dedicated authors and supporters will do all we can to ensure critical, timely, integrated Arctic data still makes it to the decision makers, educators, and community leaders who need it. But without federal support, the task is harder, the data access systems built over two decades will go unused a trusted data source will become stale. This puts U.S. Arctic leadership at risk.

In “ Science: A New Golden Age ,” White House Director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy Michael Kratsios writes “Never have science and technology been more central to our nation’s security and prosperity, and, although America continues to set the pace of scientific progress, global competitors are racing to challenge our leadership.”

Understanding and operating effectively in the Arctic is also a key administration priority. I agree. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Arctic Report Card was one brick in that wall of U.S. Arctic leadership and intelligence building. With the Arctic heating up, this is not the time to weaken our Arctic leadership.

Twila Moon is deputy lead scientist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center, Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences at the University of Colorado Boulder.
